newsitem.title: ITALY: Paper - OECD sees Italy, France, Germany budget gap.
newsitem.headline: Paper - OECD sees Italy, France, Germany budget gap.

text.p: Italian business daily Il Sole 24 Ore reported on Thursday that the OECD expects Italy, France and Germany to miss the EMU entry target for budget deficits this year.

In Paris, however, an OECD spokeswoman said the organisation did not accept the accuracy of the figures given for budget deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratios. The data were said to come from the OECD's latest economic report, due to be published next Wednesday.
"They are wrong," she said. "There are mistakes in the information..."
She declined any detailed comment on whether any of the Il Sole report was correct and said the OECD was sticking to the 1500 GMT June 18 release date.
Il Sole reported that the OECD forecasts put Italy's 1997 deficit to gross domestic product ratio at 3.2 percent, the same figure forecast for France and Germany.
It said the OECD forecast Italy's deficit/GDP ratio would rise to 3.8 percent in 1998 while France's ratio would fall to 3.0 percent and Germany's to 2.9 percent.
The criteria for entry to the European Union's planned economic and monetary union (EMU), due to start on January 1, 1999, set 3.0 percent as the target ceiling for budget deficits.

Il Sole said the OECD forecasts, in line with those of the European Commission, took into account the Italian government's 15.5 trillion lire March mini-budget "and its inevitable effects on public finances and growth."

But the deficit/GDP ratio would hit 3.8 percent next year if Italy did not implement further deficit-cutting measures. France, however, would see its ratio fall to the 3.0 percent level next year without any further government measures, while Germany would see 2.9 percent.
Il Sole said the OECD report noted with satisfaction that efforts among member countries to get public accounts in line were already well underway.

The report noted that the urgency for EMU candidates to get accounts in order was even greater because with the single European currency they would not be able to deal with cyclical crises by using national macroeconomic policies as they had in the past, Il Sole said.

Il Sole added that the report underlined the fact that "given the already high level of taxation and the consequent non-optimal destination of resources, many countries will have to resort to spending cuts in order to straighten out their accounts." -- Milan newsroom +392 66129589
